lessons.title: Spotting hazards and using PPE
lessons.html:
What is a hazard?

A hazard is anything that can hurt you. A risk is how likely it is to hurt you and how badly. In a tractor workshop there are many hazards. You must learn to see them and control them before you start a job.

Common workshop hazards

  • Heavy parts and machines that can fall or roll
  • Moving parts: fans, belts, PTO shafts, augers
  • Hot parts: exhausts, engines, turbos, coolant
  • Fluids under pressure: hydraulics, fuel, coolant, tyres
  • Electricity: batteries, welders, power tools, extension leads
  • Chemicals: diesel, oil, solvents, battery acid, coolant
  • Noise from grinders and hammering
  • Oil on the floor, cables and tools lying around
  • Dust, fumes and sparks

Think before you start

Before each job, stop and ask: What can go wrong? How can I stop it? What PPE do I need? This is called a task risk check. Many workshops use a short checklist for it.

Personal protective equipment (PPE)

PPEProtects against
Safety boots with steel toecapsFalling parts, crushing, slipping
OverallsDirt, oil and minor burns
Safety glassesFlying chips, splashes
Face shieldGrinding, battery acid, chemicals
GlovesCuts, chemicals, heat
Ear plugs or muffsLoud noise
Welding helmetArc light and sparks
Dust mask or respiratorDust and fumes

Check your PPE before use. Replace it if damaged. Do not wear loose clothing, rings, chains or long loose hair near moving parts. Do not wear gloves near rotating drills or lathes because they can be caught.

Report what you cannot fix

If you see a hazard you cannot make safe yourself, such as a broken guard or a damaged sling, tell your supervisor at once and warn others.

lessons.title: Safe work procedures and emergencies
lessons.html:
Safe procedures on every job

Making the tractor safe

  1. Park on level, firm ground.
  2. Lower implements and the loader to the ground.
  3. Put the transmission in park or neutral and apply the handbrake.
  4. Stop the engine and take out the key. Put a Do not operate tag on the steering wheel.
  5. Chock the wheels.
  6. Let hot parts cool down.
  7. Release hydraulic pressure as the manual shows.

Lifting and supporting

  • Use a jack only to lift. Always put the tractor on stands before you go under it.
  • Use a crane or hoist with a checked sling for heavy parts.
  • Never stand under a raised load.
  • Lift small loads with your legs and keep your back straight. Ask for help with heavy items.

Electrical safety

Check power tool cables and plugs before use. Do not use damaged extension leads. Keep cables out of water and oil. Disconnect the tractor battery before electrical work, negative first.

Housekeeping

A tidy workshop is a safe workshop. Clean spills at once with absorbent. Put tools back. Keep walkways and fire exits clear. Throw oily rags into a closed metal bin.

Fire

Know where extinguishers are and what type to use. Do not smoke in the workshop. Keep fuel away from welding and grinding. If a fire is too big, leave, raise the alarm and call for help.

Injuries and first aid

If someone is hurt: make the area safe, call the first aider and your supervisor, and call emergency services if the injury is serious. Do not move a badly injured person unless they are in danger. Report every injury and near miss, even small ones, so the cause can be fixed. First aid must be learnt hands-on from an accredited first aid training provider; this lesson does not replace that training.

Your rights and duties

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, you must follow safety rules and use PPE. Your employer must give you training, PPE and a safe workplace.

Key points

  • Do a quick risk check before every job.
  • Wear the right PPE and no loose clothing near moving parts.
  • Make the tractor safe: implements down, key out, wheels chocked.
  • Never go under a tractor held only by a jack.
  • Report every injury and near miss.
